title: Judging, Asking, and Building on the Rock
summary: Jesus warns his disciples not to judge others while ignoring the beam in their own eye, encourages them to ask, seek, and knock because their Father gives good gifts, and sums up the Law and the Prophets in the command to treat others as they would want to be treated. The sermon closes with a series of choices: the narrow gate or the wide one, true prophets or false, saying Lord, Lord or doing the Father's will, building on rock or on sand. The crowds are astonished, because Jesus teaches with authority, not like their scribes.
story: This chapter ends the Sermon on the Mount, the first of Matthew's five great discourses. Chapter 5 set out the character of kingdom people and the righteousness Jesus requires; chapter 6 taught that righteousness before the Father in secret, with the Lord's Prayer at its heart. Chapter 7 turns to relationships with others and then presses the listener to decide. Having heard the whole sermon, no one can stay neutral: every hearer is building a house, and the storm is coming. The narrator's closing comment (verses 28 and 29) introduces the next section, where Jesus comes down from the mountain and shows the same authority in deeds, healing a leper, a centurion's servant, and many others (chapters 8 and 9).
historical:
The sermon's closing section reflects the world of Jewish teaching in the first century. Rabbis and scribes taught by citing the law and the interpretations of earlier respected teachers, building on the tradition passed down to them. A famous saying attributed to Hillel, a leading teacher of the generation before Jesus, tells a would-be convert that what is hateful to you, you should not do to your neighbor, and that this is the whole law, the rest being commentary. The book of Tobit, written a century or two before Christ, has a similar negative form. Jesus' Golden Rule is stated positively, asking not only for restraint from harm but for active good.

False prophets were a real concern in the period. Josephus describes several figures in the first century AD who claimed to be prophets and led crowds into the wilderness or to the Mount of Olives with promises of deliverance, and whom Roman forces crushed. The early Christian communities also had to test traveling prophets and teachers; the Didache, an early church manual, gives instructions for recognizing false ones by their conduct. Matthew's first readers would have heard verses 15 to 23 as practical guidance.
cultural:
The images of this chapter come from daily life. A speck and a beam contrast a tiny splinter of sawdust with a heavy wooden roof beam, a deliberately comic exaggeration, and a carpenter's son would have known both. Dogs in Jewish towns were mostly scavengers, not pets, and pigs were unclean animals under the law; what is holy probably refers to meat from sacrifices, which must not be thrown to animals. The picture of a father giving his son bread and fish reflects the staple foods of Galilee around the lake, and a stone or a snake might resemble them in shape.

The two ways, one leading to life and one to destruction, was a familiar pattern in Jewish teaching (Deuteronomy 30:15-20; Psalm 1; Jeremiah 21:8), and the Didache opens with the same two-ways teaching. Sheep and wolves were the common opposites of the herding life, so a wolf in sheep's clothing is a predator disguised as one of the flock. The builders of verses 24 to 27 lived in a land where dry stream beds (wadis) could fill suddenly with torrents during the winter rains; a house on the soft sand of a wadi floor would be swept away, while a house built down to bedrock would stand.
literary: The chapter is a sequence of short sayings that gathers into a strong conclusion. Verses 1 to 12 continue the teaching with a warning about judgment (verses 1 to 5), a puzzling saying about holy things (verse 6), an encouragement to prayer argued from lesser to greater (verses 7 to 11), and the Golden Rule, which summarizes the Law and the Prophets (verse 12), echoing 5:17 and so closing the main body of the sermon. Verses 13 to 27 form the conclusion, built of four contrasting pairs: two gates and ways, two kinds of trees and fruit, two kinds of disciples, and two builders. The final parable uses exact repetition, the same storm striking both houses, so that the only difference is what each builder did with Jesus' words. The narrator's comment in verse 28, When Jesus had finished saying these things, is the formula that closes each of Matthew's five discourses.

outline.t: Do not judge: the speck and the beam
The narrow gate and the wide
Lord, Lord: doing the Father's will
The crowds astonished at his authority

doctrines.note: Jesus warns that those who judge harshly will be judged by the same measure, and he presents himself as the one who will say on that day who belongs to him. Final judgment is certain, and it examines both deeds and relationship with Christ.
Ask, seek, and knock: prayer is persistent and confident because God is a Father who gives good things to his children, far more reliably than any human parent.
Faith that saves is not merely saying Lord, Lord or even doing impressive religious works; it is hearing Jesus' words and acting on them, a life built on him.
The closing parable is wisdom teaching in the tradition of Proverbs. The wise person is the one who hears and does; the fool hears and ignores, and the outcome shows only when the storm comes.

words.note: Krino, to judge, which can mean to discern, to evaluate, or to condemn. The same chapter requires discernment about dogs and swine and false prophets, so verse 1 does not forbid all moral judgment. It forbids the self-righteous condemnation that ignores one's own faults.

Stenos, narrow or confined. The narrow gate and the narrow way picture a path that is hard to find and demanding to walk, not because God is reluctant but because it runs against the easy direction of the crowd.

Anomia, lawlessness. It literally means being without law, and Matthew uses it for a life that disregards God's will, even when it looks religious (23:28; 24:12). The workers of lawlessness in verse 23 did miracles in Jesus' name yet did not do his Father's will.

Exousia, authority, the right and power to act. The crowds notice that Jesus teaches on his own authority rather than by citing earlier teachers. The word returns at the Gospel's climax, when the risen Jesus claims all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18).

christ: The end of the sermon makes the startling scope of Jesus' claim clear. He says that on that day, the day of final judgment, people will stand before him and say Lord, Lord, and he will be the one to declare, “I never knew you; depart from Me, you workers of lawlessness!” In the Old Testament God alone is the judge of all the earth; here Jesus speaks as that judge. He also makes his own words the foundation of life: everyone who hears these words of mine and acts on them builds on the rock, a role the Old Testament gives to God himself, often called Israel's rock (Deuteronomy 32:4; Psalm 18:2). The crowds' astonishment at his authority is the right response, and the rest of the Gospel shows that authority confirmed in his miracles, his death, and his resurrection. Jesus also lived the Golden Rule perfectly, doing for others, including his enemies, what no one did for him.

hard.q: If people who prophesied and did miracles in Jesus' name can be turned away, how can anyone be sure of salvation?
hard.a:
Verses 21 to 23 are among the most sobering words in the Gospels. Jesus does not say these people lost a relationship they once had; he says I never knew you, and he identifies their problem as lawlessness, a life that did not do the Father's will despite religious activity. Interpreters from different traditions agree that the passage warns against assuming that religious words, gifts, or achievements prove a genuine relationship with Christ.

They differ on how it bears on assurance. Many in the Reformed tradition read it as describing people who were never truly converted, and hold that those who belong to Christ will persevere, showing their faith in obedience. Many Arminian and Wesleyan interpreters stress the ongoing call to faithfulness and hold that a believer can fall away, while agreeing that this passage speaks of those Jesus never knew. Roman Catholic teaching emphasizes faith working through love and cooperation with grace. Across these views, assurance rests not on spiritual performance but on being known by Jesus, trusting him, and the evidence of a life built on his words. The passage is meant to unsettle the complacent, not to terrify the humble who fear they have not done enough; the same sermon began by calling the poor in spirit blessed.

questions: Jesus tells us to remove the beam from our own eye first. Whose faults are you quickest to notice, and what might that reveal about you?
The Golden Rule asks for active good, not just avoiding harm. What would it look like to apply it to someone you find difficult this week?
Both houses face the same storm. What storms have tested what your life is built on, and what did they show?
